learn.title: Plausible can still be false
learn.body: A hallucination is generated content that is false or unsupported but may sound plausible. It can appear as an invented fact, a citation that does not exist or code that uses a nonexistent feature. Clear language is not proof of accuracy.

learn.title: Why confident mistakes happen
learn.body: A language model produces likely continuations from patterns and context. That process does not automatically check every claim against reality. A confident tone, detailed explanation or neatly structured answer can therefore accompany a mistake.

learn.title: Match the check to the claim
learn.body: Check an important factual claim against reliable sources. For a citation, confirm both that the source exists and that it supports the claim. For code, inspect it and run appropriate tests. For a calculation, recompute it with explicit rules.

learn.title: Check a suggested habit method
learn.body: A model suggests a library method for calculating a habit streak, but you do not recognize it.
steps: Pause instead of adding the unfamiliar method to the tracker.
Check the library's current official documentation for the version you use.
If the method exists, test its behavior with a short known streak.
If you cannot verify it, choose a supported approach or ask for clarification.

learn.title: Treat uncertainty honestly
learn.body: You can ask a model to identify uncertainty or provide sources, but neither request guarantees a reliable result. If supporting evidence is missing, label the claim unverified. Avoid acting on it or passing it on as established fact.
Spend more verification effort when a mistake could affect safety, money, privacy or someone's work.

questions.prompt: What is a hallucination in a language model's answer?
choices: False or unsupported content that may sound plausible
A verified quotation from a real source
questions.explanation: Hallucinated content can be detailed and fluent. Its style does not reveal whether it is supported, so important claims need evidence.

questions.prompt: A real citation is useful evidence only when its source also \_\_ the claim.
questions.explanation: A source must do more than exist. Read the relevant material and confirm that it actually supports the specific claim being made.

questions.prompt: What should you do with a confident but unfamiliar citation before trusting it?
questions.explanation: Verify that the citation exists and that its contents support the claim. Confidence and a realistic citation format are not enough.

questions.prompt: Match each AI output to an appropriate check.
pairs: Inspect it and run relevant tests
Compare it with the original source
questions.explanation: Verification should test the particular kind of output. Sources support facts and quotations, while tests and explicit calculations provide different evidence.

questions.prompt: Put the response to an unfamiliar generated code feature in order.
steps: Check documentation for the version in use
Test the feature on a small known case
Integrate only if the evidence supports it
questions.explanation: Avoid letting fluent code straight into the project. Check that the feature exists for your version, test its behavior and integrate only with supporting evidence.

questions.prompt: A generated citation points to a real article, but the article does not discuss the claim. What is the claim's status?
choices: Correct because the wording is fluent
Correct if the citation has a formal style
questions.explanation: The article's existence alone does not support the claim. The claim remains unverified by this citation and needs other suitable evidence.
